body: An ETF (exchange-traded fund) is a basket of assets you buy as a single share that trades all day like a stock - instant diversification, usually at low cost.
An index fund tracks a market index like the S&P 500 instead of trying to beat it - low fees, broad exposure, no stock-picking.
Price-to-earnings divides share price by earnings per share - a rough gauge of how much you pay for each dollar of profit.
Earnings per share is a company's profit divided by its shares outstanding - the per-share slice of the bottom line.
Market capitalisation is share price times shares outstanding - the market's price tag on the whole company.
A dividend is a slice of profit paid to shareholders, usually quarterly. Plenty of growth companies pay none and reinvest instead.
Annual dividend divided by share price, as a percent - the cash return you get just for holding the stock.
The Relative Strength Index (0-100) measures how hard a stock has been bought or sold lately. Low can mean oversold, high overbought.
Moving Average Convergence Divergence tracks momentum by comparing two moving averages - crossovers can flag a shift in trend.
Beta measures how much a stock moves versus the market. Above 1 is more volatile than the index, below 1 is calmer.
Alpha is the return above what the market would explain - the value a strategy adds on its own merit.
The Sharpe ratio measures return earned per unit of risk taken. Higher means better risk-adjusted performance.
The gap between the highest price buyers offer and the lowest sellers accept. Tighter spreads mean more liquidity.
How easily an asset can be bought or sold without moving its price. Cash is the most liquid; a tiny micro-cap is not.
How much a price swings over time. Higher volatility means bigger ups and downs - more risk and more opportunity.
Borrowing shares to sell now and buy back later, betting the price falls. Losses are theoretically unlimited.
Borrowing from your broker to buy more than your cash allows. It amplifies gains and losses - and charges interest.
A call gives the right, not the obligation, to buy a stock at a set price before a date - a bullish bet with capped downside.
A put gives the right to sell at a set price before a date - used to bet on a fall, or to insure a holding against one.
A futures contract locks in a price to buy or sell something later - used to hedge or speculate on commodities, indexes and more.
A bond is a loan to a government or company that pays interest along the way and returns the principal at maturity.
A plot of bond yields across maturities. When short yields rise above long ones (inversion), recessions have often followed.
P/B compares share price to the company's net asset value per share - a classic lens for value and for banks.
The cash a business generates after capital spending - what is actually left to reward shareholders or reinvest.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation - a rough proxy for operating cash generation.
Investing a fixed amount on a schedule regardless of price, smoothing the highs and lows out over time.
Earning returns on your returns. Small gains snowball over long periods - time in the market is the engine.
A large, established, financially sound company. The name comes from the highest-value chips in poker.
A sustained rise in prices. A bull attacks by thrusting its horns up - hence the optimistic name.
A fall of roughly 20% or more from the highs. A bear swipes its paws downward - the pessimistic counterpart.
An initial public offering is the first time a private company sells shares to the public and lists on an exchange.
The short code that identifies a listed company - AAPL for Apple, BHP for BHP - a relic of the old ticker-tape machines.
A split divides each share into more shares at a lower price. The pie is the same size; the slices are just smaller.
A share buyback is a company repurchasing its own stock, shrinking the share count and lifting earnings per share.
Buy on or after this date and you miss the next dividend - the price typically drops by about the dividend amount.
An automatic trading halt triggered by a sharp drop, built to cool panic. Born after the 1987 crash.
The VIX, or fear gauge, measures expected S&P 500 volatility over the next 30 days. It spikes when markets get scared.
A 13F is a quarterly filing of a large manager's holdings - but it lags up to 45 days and excludes short positions.
A Form 4 reports a company insider buying or selling their own stock, and must be filed within two business days.
Spreading money across assets so one loss cannot sink you. Often called the only free lunch in investing.
The New York Stock Exchange traces to the 1792 Buttonwood Agreement, signed by 24 brokers under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street.
The Nasdaq launched in 1971 as the world's first electronic stock market - no trading floor, just a network of quotes.
Wall Street is named after an actual wall the Dutch built across lower Manhattan in the 1600s.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average was created by Charles Dow in 1896 and started with just 12 companies.
The S&P 500 index of large US companies was introduced by Standard & Poor's in 1957.
John Bogle launched the first index mutual fund at Vanguard in 1976 - mocked at the time, now a multi-trillion-dollar idea.
The Black-Scholes model for pricing options was published in 1973 and reshaped modern finance.
Stock exchange is bourse in French, after the Van der Beurze family whose Bruges inn hosted traders back in the 1300s.
The stock ticker was invented in 1867, printing prices onto paper tape - the origin of the ticker-tape parade.
On 19 October 1987 the Dow fell 22.6% in a single day, its worst one-day drop - and the spark for circuit breakers.
The 1944 Bretton Woods agreement pegged world currencies to the US dollar, which stayed tied to gold until 1971.
In 1630s Holland, tulip-bulb prices soared then collapsed - often cited as the first great speculative bubble.
The Cboe introduced the VIX in 1993, giving markets a single number for expected volatility.
US stocks were quoted in fractions (eighths of a dollar) until 2001, when exchanges finally switched to decimals.
The Australian Stock Exchange was formed in 1987 by merging the six state exchanges; its Sydney roots reach back to 1871.
The S&P/ASX 200 is Australia's main benchmark, tracking the 200 largest companies listed on the ASX.
Australia's dividend imputation (franking) credits stop dividends being taxed twice - a feature few other countries share.
Australia's compulsory super system began in 1992; employers must pay a slice of wages into a retirement fund.
The Reserve Bank of Australia sets the cash rate, the interest-rate lever that ripples through mortgages and markets.
The ASX trades 10:00 to 16:00 Sydney time after a pre-open auction, and is closed on public holidays.
Australia's market leans heavily on miners and banks, so commodity prices and interest rates move the index a lot.
The ASX settles trades through CHESS, its electronic clearing system - whose long-running replacement has been quite the saga.
Since 2024 most US stock trades settle in one business day (T+1) - cash and shares change hands the next day.
Stocks can trade before and after the official session, but with thinner volume, wider spreads and bigger swings.
Underwriters gauge demand on a roadshow, set an offer price, then the stock floats - it can pop or flop on day one.
Market makers quote both a buy and sell price continuously, providing the liquidity that lets you trade instantly.
A market order fills now at the going price; a limit order only fills at your price or better.
A stop-loss order sells automatically if the price falls to a set level, capping a loss - though a gap can skip past it.
The float is the number of shares actually available to trade, excluding locked-up insider and restricted holdings.
The trade date is when you agree the deal; the settlement date is when the money and shares actually move.
Periodically trimming winners and topping up laggards to hold your target mix - selling high and buying low by rule.
Higher potential returns come with higher risk. Anything promising big returns with no risk is a red flag.
Timing the exact bottom is brutally hard; staying invested through the cycle has historically beaten jumping in and out.
A retirement rule of thumb: draw about 4% of your portfolio in year one, adjust for inflation, and it may last roughly 30 years.
The efficient market hypothesis argues prices already reflect known information, making it hard to consistently beat them.
Value investors buy below their estimate of worth, leaving a cushion if they are wrong - a Ben Graham principle.
Ben Graham pictured the market as a moody partner quoting wild prices daily - your job is to exploit his moods, not follow them.
Looking only at the funds and stocks that survived hides the failures - and quietly flatters past returns.
People feel a loss about twice as hard as an equal gain, which nudges investors to sell winners early and cling to losers.
Reinvested dividends have historically driven a large share of long-run total returns, not just the price gains.
Quants trade with maths and code instead of gut feel - many of the biggest funds are now run largely by algorithms.
The buttonwood (American sycamore) the NYSE was born under still lends its name to finance columns today.
There are far more stock indexes in the world than there are listed companies - thousands slice the market every way imaginable.
Four times a year, options and futures expire together (triple witching), often spiking volume and volatility.
The Charging Bull statue near Wall Street was installed without permission in 1989 as a piece of guerrilla art.
A brief recovery in a falling price before it drops again - traders grimly note that even a dead cat bounces if dropped far enough.
Markets show only weak, inconsistent day-of-week patterns - most calendar quirks vanish once everyone knows about them.
Every gram of gold ever mined would fit in a cube about 22 metres a side - that scarcity is the whole point.
The line that compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world is often attributed to Einstein, though it is unverified.
Frozen pork bellies were a famously traded futures contract for decades - the punchline of many trading-floor jokes.

When switching from a 5-minute chart to a 1-minute chart, you are peering inside a single 5m candle. One 5-minute candle is composed of exactly five 1-minute candles stitched together. Use the shorter 1m timeframe strictly to study initial momentum, and the 5m to see if the overall story holds.

term: The Power of the Candle Close
body: While a candle is still actively forming, it can present false signals. A price spike looks bullish on the chart, but if sellers push it back down before the time bracket expires, it leaves a long upper wick. Never commit to a setup based on an unfinished candle; wait for the official close.

Every candlestick tells a brief story through four numbers: Open, High, Low, and Close. The body represents the distance between Open and Close, while the thin wicks (shadows) mark the highest and lowest prices reached during that period. The close shows whether buyers or sellers won the final seconds.

Buying a stock just because a 1-minute candle is aggressively spiking green is a common beginner trap. If the candle is only seconds old, that momentum is unproven and easily reversed. Always wait to see if the impulse is sustained through multiple candles or confirmed on a larger timeframe.

Support is a price floor where buying interest absorbs selling pressure, while resistance is a ceiling where selling caps a price rise. The most reliable support levels are established over multiple candle closes on daily or hourly charts, rather than brief intra-day wicks on small timeframes.

Volume measures the total shares traded. When a stock breaks above resistance, high volume acts as validation, showing strong consensus. Conversely, price rises on low volume suggest weak conviction and are highly prone to reversing back into the previous range.

Paper trading allows you to test your strategies and chart reading in real-time without risking actual capital. It is the best way to practice waiting for candle closes, managing wicks, and setting proper stop-losses before putting real cash on the line.

Overtrading is the result of emotional impatience and chasing small, noisy moves on ultra-short timeframes like the 1-minute chart. Focus on high-quality setups that align with the hourly trend. Remember: doing nothing is a highly active, profitable trading decision.

Ultra-short charts (1m, 45s) are highly noisy and prone to random volatility. A massive green bar on a 1m chart may disappear on a 15m or 1h chart as a tiny, insignificant wick. Always filter out local noise by aligning your trade direction with the larger daily trend.

A stop-loss order is your absolute insurance policy. The moment the market structure invalidates your setup (such as breaking below a key higher low), exit the trade. Never hold a losing position hoping it will bounce back; hope is not a trading strategy.

A higher low pattern occurs when a stock dumps, finds a bottom, pulls back again, but holds above that initial bottom. This is the first structural sign that selling pressure is exhausted and buyers are stepping in to defend prices, reversing the previous series of lower lows.

The middle Bollinger Band represents the simple moving average. When a recovering stock reaches this line, it faces a critical decision point. A strong close above it suggests buyers are reclaiming control, while a rejection and immediate wick back down indicates continued weakness.

An RSI value under 30 indicates a stock is oversold, but a low RSI alone is not an entry trigger. Wait for the RSI to rise back above 30, and ideally cross 50, to confirm that momentum has actually shifted from bearish to neutral-bullish before entering a position.

Watch the MACD histogram for early signs of exhaustion. When the histogram is negative but begins to shrink (rising toward the zero line), it indicates that selling pressure is curling up. While not a full uptrend confirmation, this marks early reversal momentum building.

Bollinger Bands represent standard deviations. Price pushing outside the upper band is statistically extended and vulnerable. Buying here represents poor risk/reward. Instead, look for a consolidation close back inside the bands or a pullback to the middle band for entry.

Before placing any trade, calculate your target and risk level. A disciplined trader looks for at least a 2:1 risk/reward ratio, meaning the potential gain is double the potential loss. If your stop-loss is close to support, your risk is minimised and your ratio is maximised.

A wick that spikes above a key moving average or resistance level, but closes back below it, represents a failed breakout. Traders who bought during the spike are trapped. Always wait for the candle close to confirm the level has been successfully reclaimed.

To confirm a setup, check multiple timeframes. A day trader might look at the 1m for entry timing, the 5m to confirm the immediate setup structure, the 15m to see the intraday trend, and the hourly to check major levels. Never trade a small timeframe in isolation.

Don't wait for the trend to fully reverse before taking profits. When price is extended outside the upper Bollinger Band, RSI is cooked (>70), and the MACD histogram begins to shrink, scale out (trim) a portion of your position into that strength.

Adjust your position size based on the volatility of the stock. High-beta or small-cap stocks swing violently and require smaller position sizes to keep your overall portfolio risk consistent. Sizing should be driven by the distance to your logical technical stop-loss.

A breakout on standard volume is highly suspect. Look for a volume ratio above 1.5x relative to the 20-period average. This relative volume spike confirms institutional participation and validates the breakout as a high-probability continuation move.

Fakeouts occur when price breaches a resistance level, drawing in momentum buyers, only to reverse and close back inside the range. This leaves a long upper wick. The key is to wait for the candle to close above the level, verifying that supply was absorbed.

Bullish divergence happens when price makes a lower low, but the RSI makes a higher low. This indicates that even though price fell, the selling velocity is decelerating, signalling that a reversal is likely building behind the scenes.

When the MACD line pulls back toward the zero line but bounces off it, this is a strong sign of trend continuation. The zero line acts as momentum support; a bounce indicates the prevailing trend is strong and the pullback was merely healthy consolidation.

Exhaustion is signaled when three conditions align on a 5m or 15m chart: RSI is overbought (>75), price is pushed well outside the upper Bollinger Band, and the MACD histogram begins to decline. This confluence suggests the buying impulse has run out of gas.

A reclaim zone is a previous support area that was broken and turned resistance. Reclaiming it requires price to push above it and, crucially, hold above it on a subsequent pullback. If the pullback bounces off the zone, the level is confirmed as new support.

Intraday trends often exhaust at key session boundaries or when moving averages become overly stretched. If a stock has gone vertical, compare its distance from the 20-day moving average on multiple timeframes; a large gap indicates overextension.

A high-confidence momentum setup requires volume confirmation. In a reversal, look for high volume on the green impulse candles and low volume on the red pullback candles. This shows buyers are aggressive and sellers are passive.

A Bollinger squeeze happens when volatility dries up and the bands contract tightly. This indicates a massive breakout is building. Wait for a candle to close outside the bands with high relative volume to confirm the direction of the expansion.

A professional stop-loss is placed where the trade structure is proven wrong, such as just below a key higher low or support level. Calculate your position size so that the distance between your entry and this stop-loss equals exactly 1-2% of your portfolio value.

A higher low pattern is only confirmed when the price breaks above the previous swing high. Until that break occurs, the stock is merely in a range. Advanced traders enter near the higher low with tight stops, anticipating the swing high break.

Fractionalize timeframes to manage trades: use the 1h/4h to define the macro bias, the 15m to map key intraday structure, the 5m to confirm the immediate setup close, and the 1m to execute. This structured process eliminates emotional execution.

A long upper wick indicates that as price rose, it encountered a large block of passive limit sell orders or aggressive market sellers, absorbing all buying pressure and driving the price back down. Wicks are historical records of order flow rejection in real-time.

The strongest reversal setups occur when RSI divergence aligns across multiple timeframes. For example, a 5-minute bullish divergence that occurs during a 1-hour oversold condition indicates structural exhaustion, carrying an exceptionally high probability of a bounce.

Expert momentum traders track the rate of change of the MACD histogram (the derivative of the histogram). Acceleration in the slope of a negative histogram often precedes the actual MACD line crossover by several candles, letting you enter early with minimal risk.

In a strong uptrend, price will often 'ride' the upper Bollinger Band. Reversal is signaled not when price touches the band, but when a candle closes back inside the band, accompanied by an RSI bearish cross and volume contraction, indicating buy side exhaustion.

When a stock reclaims a breakdown level, watch the first retest. If the price fails to bounce and closes back below the level, it represents a 'reclaim invalidation.' This trap trigger often leads to a fast, aggressive flush as buyers are forced to cover.

Combine candle wicks with volume profile analysis. A long wick that coincides with a high-volume node on the volume profile indicates major institutional distribution or accumulation. These levels act as powerful support or resistance boundaries.

Never exit a winning position all at once. Scale out in tranches (e.g., trim 1/3 at the first overextension signal, 1/3 at a moving average cross, and let the final 1/3 run with a trailing stop). This maximises yield and keeps you aligned with structural moves.

Arbitrage timeframes by identifying where short-term noise contradicts long-term trends. If a stock is in a strong 1h uptrend, a sharp drop on the 1m chart that reaches oversold RSI levels is a low-risk accumulation opportunity, exploiting the panic of short-term traders.

A true shift in market structure occurs when a stock breaks its previous swing high on high volume. This changes the trend from bearish/neutral to bullish. Expert traders wait for a successful test of the breakout point before sizing in fully.

Executing trades during vertical, high-wick spikes on small timeframes exposes you to major slippage. Set limit orders in the liquidity pools near key moving averages rather than chasing market orders into the peak of wicks where liquidity is thin.
Don Bradman's CV goes beyond cricket: in 1943, the famous Australian cricketer became a member of the Stock Exchange of Adelaide.
On Australia's old trading floors, brokers gathered at 'posts' to deal in stocks, while 'chalkies' recorded the bid and offer prices and sales in chalk.
The Australian Stock Exchange was formed on 1 April 1987, and its SEATS automated trading system was introduced that October: the day before the global stock market crash.
The exchange that became the NYSE once rented a room at 40 Wall Street, where brokers met twice a day to trade a list of 30 stocks and bonds, shouting bids and offers from their assigned chairs.
The NYSE's famous bell was first used in the 1870s, with the advent of continuous trading. But the original bell of choice wasn't a bell at all: it was a Chinese gong.
On 28 December 1967, Muriel Siebert became the first woman to hold a seat on the New York Stock Exchange in its 175-year history, and the only woman among 1,365 men.
The London Stock Exchange's story starts in a coffee house: in 1698, at Jonathan's Coffee House, John Castaing began issuing a price list called 'The Course of the Exchange and other things'.
The Chicago Mercantile Exchange has breakfast-table roots: its predecessor, the Chicago Butter and Egg Board, was founded in 1898.
When the Dow Jones Industrial Average was first calculated, it was made up of just 12 industrial companies, and the average started at 40.94 points.
The first Dow index wasn't the Industrial Average. It was the 1884 Dow Jones Railroad Average of 11 stocks, published in the Customer's Afternoon Letter, the precursor to The Wall Street Journal.
When The New York Times began publishing Standard & Poor's new index of 500 stocks, it said the gauge was made possible by 'the marriage of a stock market ticker with an electronic computer'.
Edison didn't invent the stock ticker. The credit goes to Edward Calahan, who devised the first one in 1867; Edison developed his Universal Stock Printer in 1871.
US share prices once moved in fractions. When the markets converted to decimals, the minimum price increment shrank from one-sixteenth of a dollar, or 6.25 cents, to one cent.
The NYSE had no circuit breakers in place in October 1987. A working group then recommended a one-hour trading halt after a 250-point drop in the Dow, and a two-hour halt after a 400-point drop.

The RBA started life as the Commonwealth Bank: the Reserve Bank Act 1959 renamed it, with a newly created Commonwealth Banking Corporation to operate as a trading bank. The RBA commenced operations on 14 January 1960.

term: Why the RBA is in Sydney
body: The RBA put its headquarters in Sydney rather than Canberra on purpose: the aim was to maintain its independence from the political sphere. It moved into Martin Place in early 1965.

A secret November 1910 meeting on Jekyll Island, Georgia, was organised by financiers and bankers keen to begin work on a US central bank. They used only first names and told others they were on a duck hunting trip.
The Bank of England's £1.2 million founding target was raised in just 11 days by 1,268 members of the public. It was established by Royal Charter on 27 July 1694.

term: The New York Fed's gold vault
body: The New York Fed's gold vault rests on the bedrock of Manhattan Island, 80 feet below street level and 50 feet below sea level. That bedrock is what lets it support the weight of the gold.
source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

body: Woolworths began as the 'Woolworths Stupendous Bargain Basement' in Sydney's Imperial Arcade, opening on 5 December 1924. Founding CEO Percy Christmas declared: 'Every city needs a Woolworths.'
When Brambles bought the CHEP equipment pool from the Australian government in 1958, it was after the cranes and forklifts. The pallets were a bonus.
Wesfarmers began trading in 1914 from two small rooms at 13 Howard Street, Perth, as The Westralian Farmers Limited. 'Wesfarmers' was its telegraphic address.
The first glass of Coca-Cola was poured at Jacobs' Pharmacy in Atlanta on 8 May 1886. In its first year, it served about nine drinks a day.

Around 1,000 names were proposed for Australia's decimal currency, including the Oz, the Roo, the Kwid and the Ming - Menzies' nickname. In 1963 it was named the Royal; opposition saw it changed to the Dollar three months later.
To help Australians adjust to decimal currency, ads starred an animated character called Dollar Bill, whose catchy conversion jingle - sung to the tune of 'Click Go the Shears' - was an instant hit.

Australia's original 50c coin was 80% silver. The Mint stopped striking it in March 1968 as silver rose above its face value, though the metal for all 36.5 million coins had been bought before prices rose.
In January 1988, Australia marked its bicentenary with a polymer $10 note, using banknote technology developed by the Reserve Bank and CSIRO. Its successful issue was a world first.
Australia's newer banknotes can be told apart by touch: raised bumps on the long edges number one on the $5, two on the $10, three on the $20, four on the $50 and five on the $100.

To ease a colonial coin shortage, Governor Macquarie had the centres cut from Spanish dollars, making two coins: the 'holey dollar', worth 5 shillings, and the 'dump', worth one shilling and threepence.
Australia's first branch of the Royal Mint began operating in 1855 in part of Sydney's Rum Hospital, striking the country's first gold sovereigns and half sovereigns.

term: What a US note is made of
body: A US banknote is a blend of 75% cotton and 25% linen, and it would take 4,000 double folds, forwards and backwards, to tear one.

A US 5-cent note once carried the portrait of Spencer Clark, causing a public uproar - and it is unclear how it got there. In 1866, Congress banned the likeness of any living person on currency notes.

In 1933, the US restricted private use of gold, so businesses had to apply to the Fed for gold bars. On 26 July 1933, a dental manufacturer asked the Cleveland Fed for $10,000 in pure gold and was sent twenty-nine bars.

The Bank of England's nickname, the 'Old Lady of Threadneedle Street', comes from a 1797 James Gillray cartoon of Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger wooing an old lady - while really after her gold.
Some Bank of England notes are worth £1 million ('Giants') or £100 million ('Titans'). They are held as backing for the banknotes that banks in Scotland and Northern Ireland issue.
'Mortgage' comes from the Old French 'mort gage', meaning 'dead pledge'. The preferred alternative, where the property's profits went to paying off the debt, was the 'vif gage' - the 'living pledge'.
'Bankrupt' comes from the Italian 'banca rotta', a broken counter - from the practice of breaking the counters of bankrupt bankers. A 'banca' was a moneychanger's table.
A budget started out as a bag. The word comes from the Middle English 'bouget', a wallet, from the Old French 'bougette', a diminutive of 'bouge', meaning a leather bag.
'Money' comes from the Latin 'moneta', meaning mint or coinage. Moneta was an epithet of Juno, and money was coined at the temple of Juno in Rome.
'Fee' comes from the Old English 'feoh', which had three meanings: cattle or livestock, goods or possessions, and money.
The word 'dollar' traces back to Joachimsthal, or 'Saint Joachim's Valley', in Bohemia, where the local ruler turned newly found silver into large coins nicknamed Joachimsthalers.
One theory traces the market 'bear' to 1709, when it was shorthand for a 'bearskin jobber' - a title from a proverb about selling bearskins before catching the bear.
source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

body: In colonial New South Wales, promissory notes were nicknamed 'shinplasters' - paper currency thought to be worth only soaking in vinegar as a dressing for bruises.
The colony's first bank, the Bank of New South Wales, opened in Sydney's Macquarie Place in 1817, in premises leased from businesswoman Mary Reibey - who later appeared on the $20 note.

When the Bank of New South Wales merged with the Commercial Bank of Australia in 1982, neither wanted to be the only one losing its name. So they created a new one: Westpac, short for 'Western Pacific'.

The Commonwealth Bank's first branch opened at 317 Collins Street, Melbourne, on 15 July 1912 with 12 staff. Its 1916 Sydney head office became known as the 'money box' building: the bank's money box was modelled on it.

The Superannuation Guarantee Charge, introduced in 1992, required employers to contribute a minimum of 3% of employees' earnings to super. Between 1988 and 1993, super coverage of employed people rose from 51% to 80%.
Building societies began in provincial England, but colonial Melbourne embraced them: by the 1870s, membership was more than twice as high per capita as in England.
